## Proof

Let $g(z) = f(z) - f'(z)$. Since $f$ is entire (analytic on all of $\mathbb{C}$), so is $f'$, and hence $g$ is entire.

On $\mathbb{R}$, by hypothesis $f(x) = f'(x)$ for every real $x$, so $g(x) = 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

The set $\mathbb{R}$ has accumulation points in $\mathbb{C}$, and $g$ is entire. By the identity theorem, since $g$ vanishes on a set with an accumulation point in its domain, $g \equiv 0$ on all of $\mathbb{C}$.

Therefore $f'(z) = f(z)$ for all $z \in \mathbb{C}$.

The general solution to $f' = f$ is $f(z) = Ce^{z}$ for some constant $C \in \mathbb{C}$. Since $f$ is nonconstant, $C \neq 0$.

Now use the real-valued condition: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$,
$$f(x) = Ce^{x} \in \mathbb{R}.$$
Since $e^{x} > 0$ is real and nonzero, $C = f(x)/e^{x}$ must be real. Thus $C \in \mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$.

Compute the ratio:
$$f\!\left(i\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = Ce^{i\pi/2} = C \cdot i,$$
$$f(i\pi) = Ce^{i\pi} = C \cdot (-1) = -C.$$

Hence
$$\frac{f(i\pi/2)}{f(i\pi)} = \frac{Ci}{-C} = -i.$$

The constant $C$ cancels, so the answer is independent of the particular function.

$$\boxed{-i}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
